title: The Minimum-Payment Trap
primary_metric: total interest paid, in dollars, over the eighteen months before Priya's planned mortgage pre-approval conversation, comparing paying only the required minimum each month (The Minimum Track) against paying a fixed $309.20 every month regardless of how far the required minimum drops (The Fixed Push)

options.B: The Fixed Push -- tap "Pay other amount" every month and enter the fixed $309.20 payment from Appendix C, holding it constant even as the required minimum drops below it

sources.note: LendingTree's own analysis of anonymized credit reports from 400,000+ users; the page states 'the national average card debt among Americans with any type of debt in Q1 2026 was $7,756, up 1.9% from $7,615 in Q1 2025.' MEDIUM rather than HIGH because it is a well-attributed private aggregator, not a government statistical release, and it is a population average used here as a representative starting balance for one fictional cardholder, not a measurement of Priya's specific account.

sources.title: The Consumer Credit Card Market 2025
sources.note: Primary federal regulator report (the seventh biennial CARD Act report to Congress), published 2025-12-30, covering 2024 market data. Report states the average APR for general-purpose cards 'reached 25.2 percent, the highest since 2015.' Real APRs vary substantially by cardholder credit tier; 25.2% is the reported market average, used here as Priya's card's APR.

sources.claim: Minimum payment formula: greater of a flat $40 floor, or 1% of statement balance plus that cycle's accrued interest and any late fees
sources.units: USD floor / percent of balance plus interest
sources.title: How To Calculate Your Minimum Credit Card Payment
sources.note: Primary source: a major card issuer's own published minimum-payment formula, quoted directly: 'a flat fee of $40 or 1% of your statement balance, plus any interest and late fees since the last billing cycle -- whichever is greater' (with an exception that a balance under $40 is paid in full). The same page discloses that formulas vary by issuer -- percentage-only methods (1-3% of balance), flat-fee-only methods ($25, $35, or another fixed amount), and interest-plus-percentage methods (Chase's own, used here) are all real, documented variants. This case adopts Chase's formula as the representative real-world version rather than averaging across issuers, which no single source publishes as one number.

sources.claim: CARD Act requirement that every statement disclose a fixed monthly payment amount that would clear the shown balance in 36 months, and the derived dollar value of that payment for Priya's Appendix A balance and APR
sources.title: Regulation Z, Appendix M1 to Part 1026 -- Repayment Disclosures
sources.note: The regulation itself (a primary federal source) requires issuers to calculate and disclose, on every statement, 'the estimated monthly payment amount that would be required to pay off the outstanding balance shown on the statement within 36 months' plus the total 36-month cost and the interest savings versus paying only the minimum -- this is a real, mandatory disclosure box, not a case-invented framing. The specific $309.20 dollar figure is DERIVED, not itself published anywhere: it is the standard fixed-payment amount that amortizes S1's $7,756 balance at S2's 25.2% APR over exactly 36 months, computed as balance x monthly_rate / (1 - (1+monthly_rate)^-36) = 7756 x 0.021 / (1 - 1.021^-36) = $309.1982, rounded to $309.20. Verifying this payment amount clears the balance to exactly $0.00 at month 36 is shown in RESEARCH_LOG.md. This computation is deliberately NOT one of the case's graded deliverables (see case-write's 'not a plugged amortization formula' framing) -- it is given to the student as a fact the real card statement would already show, the same way a real disclosure box hands a cardholder this number without requiring her to derive it herself.

An eighteen-month month-by-month table for EACH strategy, built by iterating the D1 recursive formula one month at a time: month number, that month's interest charged, that month's payment, how much of the payment went to principal, and the ending balance -- every row computed from the PREVIOUS row's ending balance, never from Appendix A's original balance.

An eighteen-month totals comparison, summed from the D2 tables: total interest paid and total principal paid under each strategy over the eighteen months, plus the percent margin between the two strategies' eighteen-month interest totals, with the arithmetic shown.

Continuing the D1 recursive model past month eighteen, find how many total months (and years) The Minimum Track takes to reach a $0 balance and the total interest paid over that ENTIRE payoff, contrasted with The Fixed Push's own total months and total interest to reach $0. A written explanation, using the D1 model, of why estimating either payoff time by charging interest only on Appendix A's original balance for every month (instead of recalculating it on each month's own ending balance) produces a wrong answer, and in which direction it is wrong.
A percent breakdown for each strategy's eighteen-month totals from D3: of every dollar paid, what percent went to interest and what percent went to principal.
An original visual display (a line graph or bar chart) comparing the two strategies' month-by-month balances across the eighteen months, built from the D2 figures.

appendices.title: How Her Minimum Payment Is Calculated

balance.argument_a: The Minimum Track keeps far more cash in Priya's pocket every single month: its required payment starts at $240.44 (month 1) and keeps shrinking (down to $202.67 by month 18) as the formula recalculates off a smaller balance, versus The Fixed Push's flat $309.20 with no exceptions. Summed over the eighteen months, The Minimum Track demands $3,978.88 in total payments versus The Fixed Push's $5,565.57 -- a real $1,586.69 kept in Priya's budget over the same window, which matters directly given that a cut in hours is exactly what put this balance on the card in the first place (SEE BACKGROUND). A's case is a liquidity-protection argument: it is not the cheaper option on interest, but it is the option that survives another income shock.
balance.argument_b: The Fixed Push pays $290.79 less in interest over the same eighteen months ($2,404.58 vs. $2,695.37, a 10.8% margin) and, more importantly for Priya's actual eighteen-month goal, leaves a dramatically lower balance at the exact moment she and her partner sit down with a lender: $4,595.01 remaining under The Fixed Push versus $6,472.49 remaining under The Minimum Track -- a real, computed $1,877.48 difference in exactly the number a mortgage lender will look at. B's case is that the primary metric she actually cares about at month 18 is not the interest margin alone, it is the balance itself, and only a fixed, non-shrinking payment gets that balance down meaningfully in the time she has.
balance.margin_basis: margin = |interest_18mo(A) - interest_18mo(B)| / max(interest_18mo(A), interest_18mo(B)). Both totals come from iterating case.json's own recursive model (see sensitivity_model.py) starting at Appendix A's $7,756 balance, 25.2% APR (monthly rate 2.1%): interest_18mo(A), The Minimum Track, sums each month's balance_(n-1) x 0.021 where payment_n = max(0.01 x balance_(n-1) + interest_n, 40) -- total $2,695.37. interest_18mo(B), The Fixed Push, sums the same monthly interest formula but with payment_n fixed at $309.20 every month -- total $2,404.58. margin = |2695.37 - 2404.58| / 2695.37 = 290.79 / 2695.37 = 10.8%. This is within the SPEC SS2 target 10-15% band. The eighteen-month window is a stated narrative reference point (Priya's own mortgage-conversation timeline, SEE BACKGROUND), not an empirical figure -- comparing LIFETIME total interest instead (a real, sourced, and dramatically lopsided figure: $14,465.14 over 19.42 years for A vs. $3,375.11 over 3 years for B) would blow far past the SPEC SS2 20% cap, because a shrinking-minimum payment structurally cannot match a fixed payment's payoff speed over the full life of the balance -- see RESEARCH_LOG.md and FACILITATOR.md for why the eighteen-month reference point is the correct graded comparison rather than an engineered one.
